subject: DI02000121

title.en: Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T) - Limits and Fits
title.gu: Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T) - Limits and Fits

intro_text.en: Unit 3 of Mechanical Drafting (DI02000121) covers limits and fits - the dimensional-accuracy system that makes interchangeable manufacture possible. It defines limits, tolerance, deviations and allowance; explains tolerance grades and fundamental deviations; compares the hole-basis and shaft-basis systems; classifies clearance, interference and transition fits; and works the numerical calculation of fits, which the official syllabus makes compulsory in the examination.
intro_text.gu: Unit 3 of Mechanical Drafting (DI02000121) covers limits and fits - the dimensional-accuracy system that makes interchangeable manufacture possible. It defines limits, tolerance, deviations and allowance; explains tolerance grades and fundamental deviations; compares the hole-basis and shaft-basis systems; classifies clearance, interference and transition fits; and works the numerical calculation of fits, which the official syllabus makes compulsory in the examination.

h.en: 3.1 Importance of limits and fits: interchangeable manufacture
h.gu: 3.1 Importance of limits and fits: interchangeable manufacture

body.en:
Why no part is made to an exact size

No manufacturing process can produce a size exactly (a lathe, drill or grinder always leaves small errors, and measurement itself is limited). Drawings therefore do not demand one exact size; they permit every dimension to vary between two limits - the largest and smallest acceptable sizes. A part inside its limits is accepted; outside, rejected. This is the foundation of interchangeability: any shaft from a batch assembles with any hole of the mating batch, without hand-fitting - the system that makes mass production, spare parts and assembly lines possible.

The vocabulary (definitions the exam asks)

  • Basic (nominal) size: the size from which limits are derived (the design size, e.g. 50 mm), common to hole and shaft.
  • Limits of size: the two permitted extremes - maximum limit (larger) and minimum limit.
  • Tolerance: the difference between the two limits = the permitted variation (always positive). It is also the manufacturing inaccuracy the designer allows: tighter tolerance = better, slower, costlier process (turning ~ IT11-13, grinding ~ IT5-7).
  • Deviation: the algebraic difference between a limit and the basic size. Upper deviation (ES for hole, es for shaft) = max limit - basic size; lower deviation (EI, ei) = min limit - basic size. The deviation nearer the basic size is the fundamental deviation - it fixes the position of the tolerance zone.
  • Allowance: the intentional difference between mating parts at their tightest condition = the designer's chosen looseness/tightness of the fit (min clearance, or max interference with negative sign).
  • Fit: the relationship (looseness/tightness) between assembled hole and shaft of the same basic size, decided by their tolerance zones (Card 3.4).

h.en: 3.1 Tolerance grades and fundamental deviation: reading 50H7/g6
h.gu: 3.1 Tolerance grades and fundamental deviation: reading 50H7/g6

body.en:
Two independent choices define a toleranced size

The ISO/BIS limits-and-fits system specifies a size by where its tolerance zone sits (fundamental deviation, a letter) and how wide it is (tolerance grade, a number):

  • Tolerance grade (IT number): IT01, IT0, IT1 ... IT16 - 18 grades of accuracy. Smaller number = smaller tolerance = higher precision. IT5-IT7 for precision fits (grinding/lapping), IT7-IT9 general engineering fits (reaming/turning), IT11-IT13 rough work (drilling, casting). The grade depends on the basic size step: for dia. 50 mm, IT6 = 16 um, IT7 = 25 um, IT8 = 39 um.
  • Fundamental deviation (letter): capital letters A-ZC for holes, small letters a-zc for shafts. The letter positions the zone relative to the zero line: for shafts, a-h zones lie below (clearance side), j-k astride, m-zc above (interference side); holes mirror this.

Reading a fit designation (worked decoding)

Fit written on assembly drawing: dia. 50 H7/g6 -> hole 50 H7 paired with shaft 50 g6
Hole H7: letter H means EI = 0 (zone starts on the zero line); grade 7 at 50 mm = 25 um -> hole limits 50.000 / 50.025 mm
Shaft g6: letter g gives es = -9 um; grade 6 = 16 um, so ei = -9 - 16 = -25 um -> shaft limits 49.991 / 49.975 mm

Every symbol on a production drawing decodes this way - the drawing never writes the limit sizes unless needed; the fitter/inspector reads the tables. Numericals 3.1-3.3 do the complete arithmetic for the three fit types.

title.en: 3.1 Basis systems and types of fits
title.gu: 3.1 Basis systems and types of fits

body.en:
The question every fit system answers

To get all the fit variety (loose running to press fit) one member can be kept standard and the other varied. Which member is 'standard' defines the system:

  • Hole-basis system: the hole is always the H hole (EI = 0 - its lower deviation sits on the zero line) and the required fit is obtained by choosing the shaft's deviation letter (g for clearance, k for transition, p for interference...). This is the preferred, dominant system: holes are produced by fixed-size tools (drills, reamers, broaches, plug gauges) that are expensive to vary, while a shaft is easily turned or ground to any size and measured with a micrometer.
  • Shaft-basis system: the shaft is always the h shaft (es = 0) and the hole letter varies. Used where one long standard shaft (bright bar) carries several different fits along its length, or with bought-out standard shafts/bearings - changing the hole is then unavoidable.

Designation

On assembly drawings the fit is written as a fraction-like pair, e.g. dia. 50 H7/g6 (hole-basis) or dia. 50 G7/h6 (shaft-basis). Remember the anchor letters: H hole has EI = 0; h shaft has es = 0 - in examinations, spotting the H or h immediately names the system.

h.en: 3.1 Types of fits: clearance, interference, transition
h.gu: 3.1 Types of fits: clearance, interference, transition

body.en:
Three families (zone positions decide everything)

  • Clearance fit: the hole zone is entirely above the shaft zone - the shaft is always smaller, leaving a gap (clearance). Min clearance = EI(hole) - es(shaft); max clearance = ES(hole) - ei(shaft); both positive. Uses: rotating/sliding pairs - bearings, pistons, pulleys on shafts (H7/g6, H8/f7...).
  • Interference fit: the hole zone is entirely below the shaft zone - the shaft is always bigger and must be forced/shrunk in, giving a permanent grip. Computed as interferences (both positive when zones are read shaft-minus-hole). Uses: bearing races on shafts, gear hubs, dowel/press fits (H7/p6, H7/s6...).
  • Transition fit: the zones overlap - an individual pair may assemble with slight clearance or slight interference depending on the actual sizes made. Uses: accurate location with possible dismantling - dowel locations, coupling spigots (H7/k6, H7/n6...).

The one-line test

Compute min and max 'clearance' (hole minus shaft) over the limits: both positive = clearance fit; both negative = interference fit (report as interferences); opposite signs = transition fit. Numericals 3.1-3.3 work one of each, and the compulsory exam numerical of this unit is always of this kind - practise the sign discipline, not just the arithmetic.

h.en: Q1. Define: basic size, tolerance, deviation, allowance. Why are limits necessary?
h.gu: Q1. Define: basic size, tolerance, deviation, allowance. Why are limits necessary?

body.en:
Model answer

Basic size is the design size from which all limits are derived, common to the mating hole and shaft. Tolerance is the permitted variation of a size - the difference between its maximum and minimum limits, always positive. Deviation is the algebraic difference between a limit and the basic size: upper deviation (ES/es) from the maximum limit, lower deviation (EI/ei) from the minimum limit. Allowance is the intentional difference designed between mating parts at their tightest condition - the minimum clearance (or maximum interference) of the fit. Limits are necessary because no process makes an exact size economically; specifying two acceptable limits permits manufacture and objective inspection, and matching hole/shaft limits is what creates interchangeable assembly without hand-fitting.

h.en: Q2. Differentiate between hole-basis and shaft-basis systems. Which is preferred and why?
h.gu: Q2. Differentiate between hole-basis and shaft-basis systems. Which is preferred and why?

body.en:
Model answer

In the hole-basis system the hole is always made to the H deviation (lower deviation EI = 0) and the fit is obtained by varying the shaft size; in the shaft-basis system the shaft is always h (upper deviation es = 0) and the fit is obtained by varying the hole. Hole-basis is preferred in industry because holes are produced and gauged by standard fixed-size tools - drills, reamers, broaches and plug gauges are costly to make in many sizes - whereas a shaft can be turned or ground to any size cheaply and measured with micrometers over its whole range. Shaft-basis is retained for long standard shafts carrying several fits and for assemblies built around bought-out standard bars or bearings.

h.en: Q3. Explain clearance, interference and transition fits with one application each.
h.gu: Q3. Explain clearance, interference and transition fits with one application each.

body.en:
Model answer

A clearance fit has the hole tolerance zone wholly above the shaft zone, so a positive gap always exists between assembled parts - e.g. a journal running in a bearing (50 H7/g6). An interference fit has the hole zone wholly below the shaft zone, so the shaft is always oversize and the joint grips permanently after pressing or shrink-fitting - e.g. a bearing inner race forced onto a shaft (50 H7/p6). A transition fit has overlapping zones, so a particular pair may end with slight clearance or slight interference - e.g. a coupling spigot that must locate accurately yet be dismantlable (50 H7/k6). The fit type is decided purely by the relative positions of the two tolerance zones about the zero line.

h.en: Q4. For 50 H7/g6, the deviations are: hole ES = +25 um, EI = 0; shaft es = -9 um, ei = -25 um. Calculate the limit sizes and the maximum and minimum clearance. Name the fit. (Compulsory-type numerical)
h.gu: Q4. For 50 H7/g6, the deviations are: hole ES = +25 um, EI = 0; shaft es = -9 um, ei = -25 um. Calculate the limit sizes and the maximum and minimum clearance. Name the fit. (Compulsory-type numerical)

body.en:
Model answer

Hole limits: max = 50 + 0.025 = 50.025 mm; min = 50.000 mm. Shaft limits: max = 50 - 0.009 = 49.991 mm; min = 50 - 0.025 = 49.975 mm. Maximum clearance = largest hole - smallest shaft = 50.025 - 49.975 = 0.050 mm (50 um). Minimum clearance = smallest hole - largest shaft = 50.000 - 49.991 = 0.009 mm (9 um). Both clearances are positive, so it is a clearance fit (easy running/sliding fit). Full working is in Numerical 3.1.

h.en: Q5. What is tolerance grade? How does the grade number relate to accuracy and cost?
h.gu: Q5. What is tolerance grade? How does the grade number relate to accuracy and cost?

body.en:
Model answer

Tolerance grade (IT number, IT01 to IT16) specifies the width of the tolerance zone for a given basic-size step: it is the quality of accuracy, independent of where the zone sits (which the deviation letter fixes). Smaller grade numbers mean smaller tolerance and higher accuracy - IT5-IT7 come from grinding/lapping, IT7-IT9 from fine turning/reaming, IT11-IT13 from ordinary drilling or casting. Cost rises steeply as grade number falls, because finer processes, slower feed, better machines and more inspection are needed; a designer therefore chooses the loosest grade that still lets the part function.

h.en: Q6. What is fundamental deviation? How is it identified for an H hole and an h shaft?
h.gu: Q6. What is fundamental deviation? How is it identified for an H hole and an h shaft?

body.en:
Model answer

The fundamental deviation is the deviation (upper or lower) that is closer to the basic size - it positions the tolerance zone relative to the zero line and is designated by a letter (capital for holes, small for shafts). For an H hole the fundamental deviation is the lower deviation, EI = 0: the zone starts exactly on the zero line. For an h shaft the fundamental deviation is the upper deviation, es = 0. These two anchor cases define the hole-basis and shaft-basis systems respectively.

h.en: Q7. State two advantages of interchangeable manufacture.
h.gu: Q7. State two advantages of interchangeable manufacture.

body.en:
Model answer

(1) Assembly without fitting: any part from a batch fits any mating part, so assembly lines run fast and unskilled fitting labour is eliminated. (2) Easy maintenance and spares: a worn component is replaced by a standard spare made years later by any manufacturer, because both honour the same limits. (Also acceptable: mass production in different plants/countries, objective inspection by limit gauges.)
body.gu:
Model answer

(1) Assembly without fitting: any part from a batch fits any mating part, so assembly lines run fast and unskilled fitting labour is eliminated. (2) Easy maintenance and spares: a worn component is replaced by a standard spare made years later by any manufacturer, because both honour the same limits. (Also acceptable: mass production in different plants/countries, objective inspection by limit gauges.)

h.en: Q8. A fit gives maximum clearance +23 um and maximum interference 18 um. Classify the fit and justify.
h.gu: Q8. A fit gives maximum clearance +23 um and maximum interference 18 um. Classify the fit and justify.

body.en:
Model answer

It is a transition fit. Depending on the actual sizes produced within their limits, a pair may assemble with up to 23 um clearance or require up to 18 um of interference (light pressing). Mixed signs of the extreme clearances are the signature of overlapping tolerance zones, which is the definition of the transition family (worked fully in Numerical 3.3, 50 H7/k6).

title.en: Numerical 3.1 - Clearance fit calculation: dia. 50 H7/g6
title.gu: Numerical 3.1 - Clearance fit calculation: dia. 50 H7/g6

body.en:
Given

Fit dia. 50 H7/g6. From the standard tables for the 50 mm size step: hole H7: ES = +25 um, EI = 0. Shaft g6: es = -9 um, ei = -25 um.

Find

Limit sizes of hole and shaft; maximum and minimum clearance; type of fit.

Formula

Limit = basic size + deviation ; Max clearance = ES - ei ; Min clearance = EI - es (hole minus shaft, deviations in um)

Substitution and calculation

Hole: max = 50.025 mm, min = 50.000 mm (tolerance 25 um)
Shaft: max = 50 + (-0.009) = 49.991 mm ; min = 50 + (-0.025) = 49.975 mm (tolerance 16 um)
Max clearance = 50.025 - 49.975 = 0.050 mm = 50 um
Min clearance = 50.000 - 49.991 = 0.009 mm = 9 um
50 H7/g6 is a CLEARANCE fit: clearance varies from 9 um to 50 um (allowance = 9 um)

Validity check

Both extreme clearances positive, so every shaft runs free in every hole ✓; zone diagram drawn in md3_example. Sign discipline: clearances are always computed hole-minus-shaft; a negative result would mean interference.

title.en: Numerical 3.2 - Interference fit calculation: dia. 50 H7/p6
title.gu: Numerical 3.2 - Interference fit calculation: dia. 50 H7/p6

body.en:
Given

Fit dia. 50 H7/p6. Hole H7: ES = +25 um, EI = 0. Shaft p6: ei = +26 um, es = +42 um.

Find

Limit sizes; maximum and minimum interference; type of fit.

Formula

Interference = shaft size - hole size at the compared limits ; Max interference = es(shaft) - EI(hole) ; Min interference = ei(shaft) - ES(hole)

Substitution and calculation

Hole: 50.000 to 50.025 mm ; Shaft: min = 50.026 mm, max = 50.042 mm
Max interference = 50.042 - 50.000 = 0.042 mm = 42 um
Min interference = 50.026 - 50.025 = 0.001 mm = 1 um
50 H7/p6 is an INTERFERENCE fit: interference varies from 1 um to 42 um - permanent press/shrink assembly

Validity check

Even the loosest pair (smallest shaft in largest hole) still interferes by 1 um ✓, so the joint grips in every case - exactly what a press fit must guarantee; assembly needs a press or thermal expansion, never hand assembly.

title.en: Numerical 3.3 - Transition fit calculation: dia. 50 H7/k6
title.gu: Numerical 3.3 - Transition fit calculation: dia. 50 H7/k6

body.en:
Given

Fit dia. 50 H7/k6. Hole H7: ES = +25 um, EI = 0. Shaft k6: ei = +2 um, es = +18 um.

Find

Maximum clearance and maximum interference; classify the fit.

Formula

Max clearance = ES(hole) - ei(shaft) ; Max interference = es(shaft) - EI(hole)

Substitution and calculation

Hole: 50.000 to 50.025 mm ; Shaft: 50.002 to 50.018 mm
Max clearance = 50.025 - 50.002 = 0.023 mm = 23 um (largest hole, smallest shaft)
Max interference = 50.018 - 50.000 = 0.018 mm = 18 um (largest shaft, smallest hole)
50 H7/k6 is a TRANSITION fit: up to 23 um clearance or up to 18 um interference, pair by pair

Validity check

Opposite signs at the two extremes = overlapping zones ✓. Such a fit locates parts accurately (spigots, dowelled covers) yet can be dismantled with a mallet/puller - the reason transition fits dominate assembly location duty.

Clearance = hole size - shaft size (at the stated limits) ; positive = gap, negative = interference
Max clearance = ES - ei ; min clearance = EI - es ; max interference = es - EI ; min interference = ei - ES (all deviations in um, holes ES/EI, shafts es/ei)

q.en: Why can't a part be made to exact size?
q.gu: Why can't a part be made to exact size?

a.en: Every process and measurement has error; economics forbids chasing zero error. Limits specify the acceptable band instead, and inspection accepts anything inside it.
a.gu: Every process and measurement has error; economics forbids chasing zero error. Limits specify the acceptable band instead, and inspection accepts anything inside it.

q.en: Tolerance vs deviation?
q.gu: Tolerance vs deviation?

a.en: Tolerance is the width of the permitted band (max limit minus min limit, always positive). Deviation is the signed distance of a limit from the basic size.
a.gu: Tolerance is the width of the permitted band (max limit minus min limit, always positive). Deviation is the signed distance of a limit from the basic size.

q.en: Which system is preferred, hole or shaft basis? Why?
q.gu: Which system is preferred, hole or shaft basis? Why?

a.en: Hole basis: holes need fixed-size tools (drills, reamers, plug gauges) that are costly to vary, while shafts are easily turned/ground to size and micrometer-measured.
a.gu: Hole basis: holes need fixed-size tools (drills, reamers, plug gauges) that are costly to vary, while shafts are easily turned/ground to size and micrometer-measured.

q.en: What is allowance?
q.gu: What is allowance?

a.en: The designed tightest condition of the fit: the minimum clearance in a clearance fit (or maximum interference). It is the intentional looseness/tightness chosen by the designer.
a.gu: The designed tightest condition of the fit: the minimum clearance in a clearance fit (or maximum interference). It is the intentional looseness/tightness chosen by the designer.

q.en: 50 H7/k6 is which fit?
q.gu: 50 H7/k6 is which fit?

a.en: Transition: max clearance 23 um, max interference 18 um - used for accurate, dismantlable location such as coupling spigots.
a.gu: Transition: max clearance 23 um, max interference 18 um - used for accurate, dismantlable location such as coupling spigots.

q.en: How does tolerance grade affect cost?
q.gu: How does tolerance grade affect cost?

a.en: Lower IT number means smaller tolerance, needing finer machines/processes and more inspection, so cost rises sharply; designers choose the loosest workable grade.
a.gu: Lower IT number means smaller tolerance, needing finer machines/processes and more inspection, so cost rises sharply; designers choose the loosest workable grade.

q.en: What does the letter in a shaft designation tell?
q.gu: What does the letter in a shaft designation tell?

a.en: The position of the shaft's tolerance zone about the zero line: a-h give clearance-side zones, j-k sit astride it, m-zc give interference-side zones.
a.gu: The position of the shaft's tolerance zone about the zero line: a-h give clearance-side zones, j-k sit astride it, m-zc give interference-side zones.

q.en: One use each: clearance and interference fit.
q.gu: One use each: clearance and interference fit.

a.en: Clearance: journal in a bush bearing (must rotate with an oil film). Interference: bearing race pressed on a shaft or a gear hub - permanent, torque-transmitting grip.
a.gu: Clearance: journal in a bush bearing (must rotate with an oil film). Interference: bearing race pressed on a shaft or a gear hub - permanent, torque-transmitting grip.

q.en: Why must the exam numerical on limits and fits be practised with signs?
q.gu: Why must the exam numerical on limits and fits be practised with signs?

a.en: The whole classification collapses to sign discipline: interchanging ES/EI or es/ei, or subtracting shaft-minus-hole, flips clearance into interference and fails the answer.
